hops.title: Seattle crows remembered the mask
hops.text: In 2006 at the University of Washington, John Marzluff wore a fearsome mask to trap, band and release seven wild crows. Researchers also walked campus in a neutral mask, a likeness of Dick Cheney, and left the birds alone. For years afterward, crows scolded people in the trapping mask more often than people in the Cheney mask. Uncaught crows and their young joined in. On one walk, 47 of 53 crows scolded the trapping face, and the scolding spread over a kilometer. In a separate experiment, crows stared, frozen, at a mask they had learned to link with capture; scans taken afterward showed raised activity in an amygdala region.

sources.citation: University of Washington Urban@UW News. Crows hold grudges against individual humans for up to 17 years.
Cornell, H. N., Marzluff, J. M., & Pecoraro, S. (2012). Social learning spreads knowledge about dangerous humans among American crows. Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 279(1728), 499–508.
Marzluff, J. M., Miyaoka, R., Minoshima, S., & Cross, D. J. (2012). Brain imaging reveals neuronal circuitry underlying the crow's perception of human faces. PNAS, 109(39), 15912–15917.

hops.afterHeading: The key experiment: cutting one route at a time
hops.title: Playing possum is two responses, not one
hops.text: Playing possum looks like a single act: the animal lies still and looks dead. Telemetry on four free-ranging American opossums shows two responses running at once. After vigorous contact from a person or dog, the opossums lay stiff with their mouths open; heart rate fell 46 percent and breathing 30 percent, and their hearts slowed again when the dog came back, so they were still tracking it. When researchers gave atropine, which blocks the nerve signal that slows the heart, the heart-rate drop vanished, but the rigid posture stayed. The drug separated the two responses, much as the rat lesions separate freezing from the rise in blood pressure.

sources.citation: Gabrielsen, G. W., & Smith, E. N. (1985). Physiological responses associated with feigned death in the American opossum. Acta Physiologica Scandinavica, 123(4), 393–398.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: An American opossum lying motionless on forest leaves while a puzzled dog sniffs nearby.
image.caption: A drug can block an opossum's slowed heart while its stiff, motionless pose carries on.

hops.afterHeading: The slow route: the HPA loop
hops.title: A century of whale cortisol in earwax
hops.text: In the Smithsonian and London's Natural History Museum sit long plugs of earwax from fin, humpback and blue whales. Baleen whales build up earwax in bands like tree rings, and each band preserves cortisol from about six months of the whale's life. Biologists measured 1,084 bands from 20 earplugs, from museums and stranded whales, spanning 1870 to 2016. Scored against each whale's own baseline, cortisol peaked at 68 percent above it in the early 1960s, at the height of industrial whaling. During World War II, when whaling fell, the score still rose 10 percent; the authors suspect naval activity contributed.

sources.citation: Trumble, S. J., Robinson, E. M., Berman-Kowalewski, M., Potter, C. W., & Usenko, S. (2013). Blue whale earplug reveals lifetime contaminant exposure and hormone profiles. PNAS, 110(42), 16922–16926.

Trumble, S. J., Norman, S. A., Crain, D. D., Mansouri, F., Winfield, Z. C., Sabin, R., Potter, C. W., Gabriele, C. M., & Usenko, S. (2018). Baleen whale cortisol levels reveal a physiological response to 20th century whaling. Nature Communications, 9, 4587.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A banded baleen whale earplug resting on a museum tray beside a magnifying glass.
image.caption: Each band of whale earwax holds about six months of cortisol, a record that tracks the whaling era.
